Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Airbus Airbus bows to remote working demands after series of strikes Aeroplane maker said to have watered down plans to restrict working from home to one day a week Kalyeena Makortoff and agencies Fri 21 Aug 2026 07.37 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Airbus has reportedly bowed to employee demands on remote working, after a series of strikes over its chief executive’s return-to-the office orders. The world’s largest aeroplane maker is said to have watered down plans to restrict remote working to one day a week from September. At present, staff are able to work remotely for two. It was part of a high-profile campaign by Airbus’s chief executive, Guillaume Faury, to get staff back into the office, in an effort to ensure the company could meet record demand and prepare new products after hiring thousands of new staff. Faury told employees in June that while home working had been a lifeline during the Covid pandemic, the opposite was now true as Airbus needed them to share their skills in person. “I count on all of you to support this,” he said in a memo, reported by Bloomberg. But disruption caused by a series of strikes, including in Spain, France and the UK in recent months, has forced him to backtrack, according to Reuters. Managers have now been told staff can work at home an average of two days a week, in effect curbing the chief executive’s efforts. In Spain , staff have been striking on and off since July, with approximately 40% of the company’s 14,000 local workers taking part in stoppages in recent weeks over issues including remote working, transport, paid leave and salaries. There have also been sporadic protests in France and the UK over plans to force white-collar staff into the office four days a week. However, Reuters said Airbus production – which is at the heart of the European defence industry – had not been affected by the strikes. An Airbus spokesperson said: “Our objective remains the same: we aim for increased on-site presence to ensure better collective efficiency, knowledge transfer and faster decision-making. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “However, effective change requires listening to our people. Photograph: Glenn Russell/VTDigger/AP Vermont Vermont man convicted of attempted murder of three Palestinian students James Eaton, 51, faces life in prison after jury rejects insanity defense rooted in claims he was acting on orders from US and Israeli intelligence Lucy Campbell and agency Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A jury has convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defense rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from the CIA and Mossad. Jason Eaton, 51, faces up to life in prison over the November 2023 attack near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington, which left Hisham Awartani paralyzed from the waist down and wounded his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid. The jury deliberated for several hours before reaching its verdict after a week-long trial that saw testimony from the three men and psychiatric experts called by the defense and prosecution. Eaton was ordered to be held in jail pending sentencing, which has yet to be scheduled. He stared ahead blankly as the verdict was read. Awartani and Aliahmad, sitting in the front row of the courtroom gallery, smiled and hugged people around them. “Justice has been rendered for Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen. After three years of sorrow, loss, and struggle, our families finally feel relief,” the families of the three men said in a joint statement. “The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry. But it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did.” Eaton had pleaded not guilty but did not dispute that he was the shooter. His lawyers argued that he should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, pointing to his claims that the United States and Israeli intelligence agencies transmitted orders to shoot the men to him via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbors. Had he been found not guilty by reason of insanity, he could have been ordered to undergo mental health treatment. In their statement, the families said Eaton had repeatedly used “hateful” words to describe their sons during the trial. “They were not the words of a man confused about who he shot, or why. They are the words of a man who saw three young men celebrating their friendship and wearing what made them feel closer to their far away families and home – and decided to kill them because of his own prejudices. We do not need a jury to tell us why our sons were targeted. We heard it, in his own words. This was a hate crime. We have said so from the beginning.” View image in fullscreen From left: Tahseen Aliahmad, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Hisham Awatani. Photograph: Rich Price/AP Thanking their communities in Burlington and Vermont for their support and solidarity, the families added: “That solidarity has mattered even more with each passing year, because our sons’ recovery unfolded alongside the genocide and destruction of Gaza and the escalating ethnic cleansing of the West Bank . While our children fought to heal from being shot in Burlington, they watched Palestinian children lose their lives, their homes, their land, their families. We are grateful our sons’ suffering commanded attention and support. We grieve that so much Palestinian suffering never does. “Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen have spent three years rebuilding their bodies and their lives after a hateful act almost killed them. We are profoundly relieved. And we continue to work toward a world where hateful violence against Palestinians is called out for what it is – and stopped.” The shooting, a few days after Thanksgiving, shook Burlington and reverberated in the occupied West Bank, where the three men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the US for college. The shooting, which occurred weeks after the onset of Israel’s military assault on Gaza – widely condemned as a genocide – triggered calls for a hate crime investigation. But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire on Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, who were all 20 at the time. Eaton’s lawyers argued he was suffering from a delusional, psychotic disorder after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting. Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, all of whom are now 23, told jurors of their holiday weekend visit to Awartani’s grandmother’s house, a trip to a bowling alley to celebrate his twin cousins’ birthday, and the walk they took near the University of Vermont campus after dusk that ended in the shooting. Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Providence at the time, said they were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic. Two of them said they were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs. Awartani said he noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived. Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking towards them. His face was expressionless and he did not say anything. As Eaton got to about five to 10 feet away, “he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us,” said Awartani, who was paralyzed from the waist down in the attack and now uses a wheelchair. The Associated Press contributed reporting. https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: Eight months after Donald Trump almost destroyed NATO by threatening to annex Greenland — by force, if necessary — he signed what he called a “fantastic” new deal that would give the U.S. all the control and military access it needs over the Danish territory. European allies were so alarmed by Trump’s apparent determination to take the territory at the start of the year — and his threat of 25% tariffs on anyone who got in his way — that they began talking about a future for the West without America. In many ways, the transatlantic relationship has not been the same since. Tuesday’s agreement on security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, signed at the United Nations by Trump and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, ends the dispute. But what exactly is in the deal? Who will pay for it? And who are the winners and losers from months of high-stakes talks? Advertisement Advertisement Here’s POLITICO’s guide: What exactly is the deal? This new agreement, which still needs ratification by Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers, is not, in fact, completely new. Instead, it sets out to “amend and supplement” an earlier deal between the U.S. and Denmark dating back to 1951. Many experts have been saying for months that this earlier agreement gave Trump most of what he said he wanted in terms of more or less unfettered freedom to set up military bases and police the region’s security. One key difference this time is that Greenland itself is a signatory. What is in the deal? The opening part of the text reaffirms the signatories’ commitments to abide by international law, respect Danish territory, fulfill NATO’s responsibilities, and uphold the rights of Greenlanders. Much of the rest of the text focuses on American military and civilian access to Greenland and plans to establish U.S. military facilities there. Trump promised to build two “very major” bases in Greenland. According to the text released by the Danish government, the two touted new American bases aren’t entirely new either, at least in terms of their locations. One will be at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, which was the former American Bluie West One base that closed in the 1950s. And the other is Mestersvig in eastern Greenland, which is currently home to Denmark’s Sirius Dog Sled Patrol unit and would be refurbished. Advertisement Advertisement Under the deal, the U.S. military will have “free access” to air, land and sea routes on and around Greenland between the two bases. Greenland is already home to the U.S. Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 American troops are stationed to operate a ballistic missile monitoring site to protect North America from long-range missile attack. The deal also sets out how the U.S. could establish new drone warfare facilities — “unmanned military installations” — in Greenland with fast-track approval processes from the Danish and Greenlandic authorities. But Denmark and Greenland will have the final say on where such facilities should be located, or whether they are built at all. Locking out the enemy What’s also new are several clauses designed to stop potential rivals and adversaries taking a military or economic stake in Greenland in the future. It states that no non-NATO nation can open a base on the island or mine for critical minerals or rare earths without the agreement of the three signatories. The HDMS Ejnar Mikkelsen, a Royal Danish Navy patrol vessel, sails in the waters of the Nuuk fjord, Greenland, on March 6, 2026. | Florent Vergnes/AFP via Getty Images Trump has often spoken about Chinese and Russian military activities around Greenland, claiming earlier this year that, “if you take a look outside of Greenland right now, there are Russian destroyers. There are Chinese destroyers … there are Russian submarines all over the place. We’re not going to have Russia or China occupy Greenland, and that’s what they’re going to do if we don’t.” NATO officials have quietly pushed back against those claims, with one diplomat saying “we’re not seeing any Chinese activity” around Greenland, while Russian movements in the High North haven’t changed significantly and there’s little, if any, Russian presence near Greenland. Who pays? In a recent social media post, Trump said “there will be no cost to the United States,” for rebuilding bases and expanding the U.S. presence in Greenland. Advertisement Advertisement It’s unclear how that would work since the one base mentioned in the agreement was closed by the U.S. in the 1950s and the other is a small Danish installation that currently houses sled dogs. It depends on what the Pentagon would want to use the bases for, but most likely projects are new air defense and radar installations, which would come with large construction costs. Nothing in the agreement specifies cost-sharing mechanisms between the three parties to the deal. The Pentagon didn’t respond to a request for comment. Who won? At the start of this year, Denmark faced the threat of losing the territory entirely. While Europeans’ trust in the U.S. as an ally has taken a long-term hit, the immediate risk to Danish territory has now gone, according to the legal text. Instead, the deal explicitly reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination — including choosing independence from Denmark, potentially. For what it’s worth, the deal also explicitly recognizes the need to protect the “pristine” environment of the territory and Greenlanders’ cultural, social and economic rights. “Reading it, one wonders why so much fuss for so little, when this could have been done from the start,” said Grégoire Roos, program director for Europe at the Chatham House think tank in London. “I also think it’s well played from Denmark — clean and diplomatic. Some might call it the European touch.” Speaking before the deal was published, the Atlantic Council’s Daniel Fried, a former U.S. ambassador to Poland, said the deal gave Washington something it could call a win, and “allowed the U.S. to walk back from its damaging and pointless threats of aggression.” Advertisement Advertisement Will it last? One persistent concern among European diplomats and Danish officials over the past year or so has been that even when Trump wasn’t always talking about Greenland, he had not forgotten his ambitions for the U.S. to take ownership of it. In the past, Trump has not always stuck to the deals he’s made, if he felt he could get better terms — another persistent source of anxiety in European diplomatic circles. It’s possible that the biggest consideration will be White House bandwidth. With so many other priorities — from Iran, to the mid-term elections, to the next presidential race — will Trump or his allies have the time and headspace to give to re-examining these amendments to a 75-year-old deal? Jacopo Barigazzi contributed to this report.

https://www.mediafax.ro/english/grindean.text: Grindeanu calls on the PNL and UDMR to join a committed majority Following discussions with Prime Minister-designate Luca Niculescu, the PSD leader stated that his party is not interested in positions and warned that the Social Democrats will not support a government if their demands regarding the governing program and the political majority are not met. Grindeanu stated that the discussions with Luca Niculescu had two components: the future government’s program and the political framework on which it will be based. Grindeanu: Niculescu assured us that key PSD ideas will be included in the program According to the PSD leader, the prime minister-designate gave assurances that some of the measures supported by the Social Democrats will be included in the future Cabinet’s program. “Mr. Niculescu, the prime minister-designate, assured us that key ideas from the PSD’s program will be reflected in his governing program. We are waiting for this governing program to take shape so that we can ultimately see the solutions for the people and the solutions for the economy. We have expressed our willingness and conveyed to Mr. Niculescu that some of our colleagues who worked on the governing program are ready to play an active role in the coming days, through ongoing dialogue, until this program is finalized,” stated Sorin Grindeanu. The Social Democratic leader specified that the second component of the negotiations concerns the formation of the majority that would support the new Executive. “We want a committed majority, and we are not interested in positions.” Grindeanu maintained that the PSD is not making its participation in the future political structure contingent on obtaining positions in the Executive. “The second issue relates to the political aspect. Specifically, from the outset, I told the prime minister-designate that we want a committed majority and that we are not interested in positions,” stated the PSD president. In this context, Grindeanu issued an explicit appeal to the PNL and the UDMR. “That is why I am appealing in particular to the PNL and the UDMR to demonstrate political maturity and to pitch in to build a transparent majority, if they want the PSD to participate in the government or in this joint effort. If we are not included in this economic plan (…) and there is no clear commitment from the other parties, the Social Democratic Party will not hesitate to say ‘no’ to this political initiative,” Grindeanu stated. Grindeanu: “Normally, the PSD should have received the mandate” The PSD president argued that, in his opinion, the mandate to form a majority should have gone to the Social Democrats, but he emphasized that Luca Niculescu’s appointment is a reality from which the current negotiations must proceed. “Normally, the PSD should have received the mandate to form a majority to invest a government. And we could have built a majority, if you will, around the idea of change, because 80% of Romanians are asking us for this change, and lawmakers, after all, cannot ignore this demand. However, we have a nomination in the person of Mr. Niculescu. That is why my appeal is directed at the parties,” said Sorin Grindeanu. The PSD leader called on the other parties to reduce political tensions and focus on economic and social solutions. “Let them set aside their political egos and think more about the people—especially those who are watching us and expecting solutions from us. The real confrontation should not be on the political front between parties at this time. I believe the real confrontation should be over the solutions each of us presents to resolve the problems and hardships faced by Romanians,” Grindeanu continued. “What’s at stake these days is not a political victory” The PSD president insisted that negotiations to form the new government should not be turned into a contest for political gain between parties. “What is at stake these days is not a political victory of one party over another. What is at stake for all of us, ultimately, must be raising the standard of living for Romanians and breaking this political deadlock. Hence my appeal to the political parties—and, in particular, as I said, to the PNL and the UDMR—to play an active and committed role in this effort,” stated Sorin Grindeanu. He reiterated his appeal to the parliamentary parties, asking that recent disputes be set aside. “I am making this appeal in good faith—after all, on behalf of the parliamentary parties—that during these days we set aside the political conflicts which, thank God, have been more than, shall we say, the necessary amount of dynamism on the political scene. They have reached a level that, ultimately, no normal person would want. So let’s set these things aside and think about the people who voted for us,” said the PSD leader. The PSD’s Condition for Voting on the Future Government In closing, Grindeanu stated that the PSD’s support for the future Cabinet depends on the fulfillment of the two conditions presented following the meeting with Luca Niculescu: the inclusion in the government program of measures deemed essential by the Social Democrats and the existence of a committed political majority. “So, our proposal is this: if the Social Democratic Party is to be part of the government, these two conditions must be met. Otherwise, obviously, we will not vote for a government that does not include these two elements I have announced,” stated Sorin Grindeanu. Sorin Grindeanu clarified that Ilie Bolojan’s presence at the helm of the PNL does not pose an obstacle to a potential coalition government with the Liberals and the UDMR. When asked whether the PSD would be willing to form a government with the PNL and the UDMR—and thus alongside Ilie Bolojan—the Social Democratic leader replied: “Yes, Ilie Bolojan is not a problem for Sorin Grindeanu at this time. Ilie Bolojan is the president of the PNL. It’s not my place to tell the PNL what to do. It’s up to them how they manage their affairs. What am I supposed to say about whether Ilie Bolojan is a good PNL president or not? Because we have a prime minister-designate, Luca Niculescu,” Grindeanu stated.
